ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory two-tier screening: (1) domestic: name and foundational document screening against Global Affairs Canada consolidated sanctions list (Special Economic Measures Act, United Nations Act and Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act), FINTRAC effectiveness indicators, and Canada Border Services Agency trade denial lists; (2) international: OFAC SDN and Consolidated Non-SDN list screening, EU consolidated financial sanctions list, UK OFSI consolidated list and UN Security Council consolidated list. All general partners, limited partners holding at or above 25% economic interest or control, directors, authorized signatories and ultimate beneficial owners of any partner entity must be screened. PEP checks must cover foreign PEPs, domestic PEPs under FINTRAC guidance, heads of international organizations, and close associates, with risk-based enhanced due diligence (EDD) for high-risk jurisdictions or live-traffic ad-transaction counterparties. Screening records must be retained for at least five years post-withdrawal per PCMLTFA record-keeping obligations, although the LP itself is normally not a FINTRAC reporting entity absent money services business or dealing-in-virtual-currency activity; contractual cascade to payment rails (SWIFT/ACH) must bind acquirers to maintain OFAC/FINTRAC compliance.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (operated by Service Alberta / Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction Department), accessible via authorized service providers (e.g., NuAge Registries, Secure, MyCorporation) and the NUANS (Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search) National Name Search System at nuans.com; official portal: https://www.alberta.ca/corporate-registry
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Alberta statutes require names to be stated in English or French characters (Latin alphabet). The LP name must include one of the statutory designations: 'Limited Partnership', 'L.P.', 'LP', or (in French) 'Société en commandite', 'S.E.C.', or 'SEC'. NUANS report is valid for 90 days and is mandatory before registration; all corporate and limited partnership names must be distinguishable from existing federal and provincial names within the NUANS database. Non-Latin-script UBO partner names must be transliterated phonetically into English/French for registry filings; official bilingual (English/French) forms are acceptable, and transliteration discrepancies must be reconciled by counsel.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: NUANS name report remains valid for 90 days from issuance; the Alberta Corporate Registry requires an approved NUANS report to be submitted at filing. If no filing is made within the validity period, counsel must procure a fresh NUANS report (no formal extension mechanism exists; the applicant must re-run the search). Upon name rejection, the Registrar of Corporations (Service Alberta) will issue a written objection notice. Counsel must first obtain written consent or a waiver from the conflicting registrant where they share similarity; if consent is not available, the applicant may submit a formal written appeal with legal argument to the Registrar within 30 days of the rejection notice, asserting distinctiveness and absence of confusion under the Partnership Act and Business Names Regulation. An adverse Registrar decision is appealable to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta by originating application, with interim relief possible if the name is integral to the LP's ad-exchange branding.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual or service-provider address in Alberta is legally permissible for the LP registered office, provided it is a real, physical street address within Alberta at which documents can be personally served during business hours and is publicly disclosed in the Alberta Corporate Registry. A PO Box alone is insufficient. For an in-bound programmatic ad platform (ISIC 7310), the virtual office satisfies the Partnership Act, but CRA domestic substance review and bank KYC (POCA – proof of commercial activity) may require an operating office, data-processing presence, or at minimum a physical Alberta contact and Canadian-resident service agent. The industry does not require statutory licensing (no provincial securities or broadcasting license is triggered by programmatic ad-exchange operations alone), so virtual-office risk is assessed as LOW subject to substantive CRA analysis.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: 5% per annum – unannounced physical on-site inspections are rare for Alberta LPs; CRA and Service Alberta rely on paper compliance, GST/HST records, and financial statements. Physical inspection risk rises materially (to 30%) only if the LP claims treaty benefits, passes substantial GST input tax credits, or holds导CRA relationship with high-risk payment processing corridors. For an AdTech SSP/DSP engaged via SWIFT/ACH, likelihood of government physical inspection is estimated at 5% in the first 24 months of operation.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Partnership Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c P-3, Sections 1-10
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital requirement for registration of a limited partnership in Alberta. General partners must contribute capital as per the partnership agreement.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a name search on the Alberta Corporate Registry website to ensure the proposed limited partnership name is available. If available, submit a name reservation request via the portal.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is not available or queried, select an alternative name and repeat the reservation process or amend upon filing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare and complete Form 1 - Limited Partnership Registration Statement, including details on the general partner, limited partners (if any), business activities, and registered office address. Ensure all information is accurate and signed by the general partner.
required_dossiers: Proof of identity and address for general partner
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried for missing information, provide the additional documents within the specified timeframe to avoid rejection.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the completed Form 1 electronically through the Alberta Corporate Registry portal and pay the prescribed filing fee online using a credit card or other accepted method.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the filing is rejected, receive a notice of deficiency and cure the issues by resubmitting the corrected documents within 30 days.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upon successful filing and approval, download and retain the electronic Certificate of Limited Partnership Registration. Update any internal records and commence operations.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If registration is delayed or denied, seek clarification from the registry and address any compliance issues.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada; business registration portal: Business Registration Online (bro-cra.gc.ca) and My Business Account (canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-login-services.html). For Alberta, the Alberta Corporate Tax service is administered federally by CRA, with no separate provincial sales tax authority.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Foreign limited partnership (LP) must apply for a federal Business Number (BN) and GST/HST program account using Form RC1 'Request for a Business Number' (paper) or via CRA Business Registration Online. Non-resident partnerships without a Canadian share capital or physical presence may register by mail/fax; attach Form RC1 and supporting documents. Alberta LP must also be registered with the Alberta Corporate Registry (Corporate Registry Service) and file an Alberta Partnership Annual Return. The BN serves as the statutory tax ID for GST/HST, payroll, and corporate tax accounts.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not have check-the-box elections. An LP is fiscally transparent for income tax; however, it may elect a non-calendar-year fiscal period under ITA s. 249.1(5) if certain conditions apply. For GST/HST, the partnership is a separate 'person' and may make elections under ETA s. 156 (closely related entities) and s. 177 (partnership fiscal year) if eligible. Hybrid mismatch rules under ITA ss. 18.2 and 18.3 may disallow deductions for certain payments recharacterized by foreign jurisdictions; an election under ss. 18.2(4)/18.3(3) may be available to reduce double taxation. For non-resident partners, a s. 216 election may be used to file a net rental income return.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax) administered by CRA; Alberta has no provincial sales tax, so only federal GST applies.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies) over the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters; a non-resident is not required to register unless the threshold is exceeded or the person is a platform operator required to collect GST/HST. For foreign digital services, a special domestic supplies threshold of CAD 30,000 may apply.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not require real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping, or mandatory government e-invoicing. Electronic filing of GST/HST returns via CRA's GST/HST NETFILE is mandatory for registrants with annual taxable supplies exceeding CAD 1,000,000. E-invoicing is voluntary and must comply with GAAP/CTA standards; PEPPOL and Pan-Canadian Trust Delivery Network standards are emerging.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Under ETA Schedule VI Part V, supplies of services to a non-resident recipient are generally zero-rated if the service is not performed in Canada and is not an excepted supply (e.g., advertising services may qualify if provided to a non-resident for offshore audience; the supplier must retain proof that the recipient is non-resident and the supply is for consumption outside Canada). Goods exported from Canada in accordance with the Customs Act and ETA s. 7 are zero-rated. The supplier must hold evidence satisfying the 'official or prescribed evidence' requirements under ETA s. 45 and Schedule VI Part V, ss. 7-18. Standard documentary proof includes a commercial invoice, contract, and proof of export/payment.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration, Bill of Lading, Inward Remittance Certificate
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA may reassess a zero-rated supply within the normal assessment period of four years from the date of the return; where misrepresentation, neglect or fraud is involved, the limitation period is waived. Penalties for false zero-rating claims include Excise Tax Act s. 285(1) gross negligence penalty of 50% of the net GST understated, s. 280 interest, and s. 327(1) criminal sanctions for willful evasion (up to CAD 10,000 or double the amount evaded, plus imprisonment). Retrospective disallowance of input tax credits and reversal of refunds are also applied, with no sunset for fraudulent claims.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada. Canada has no general exchange-control administration requiring routine approval for ordinary commercial foreign-exchange transactions. Applicable oversight also includes the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for anti-money-laundering compliance, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for tax reporting, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) for federally regulated financial institutions, and applicable Canadian securities regulators for derivatives and market-conduct matters.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible for ordinary current-account and capital-account transactions. Canada generally permits unrestricted receipt and remittance of investment capital, service revenue, royalties, interest, dividends, partnership distributions, and sale proceeds, subject to tax, sanctions, anti-money-laundering, beneficial-ownership, transfer-pricing, withholding, and financial-institution verification requirements. An Alberta limited partnership normally does not require prior foreign-exchange approval to receive non-resident contributions or remit distributable cash. Non-resident partners may be subject to Canadian withholding or other tax obligations depending on the character and source of income, applicable treaty relief, partnership activities, and whether the partnership carries on business in Canada. Banks may delay or reject payments pending source-of-funds evidence, beneficial-owner verification, tax documentation, sanctions screening, or explanation of unusually complex payment flows. Cross-border related-party loans, guarantees, management fees, royalties, and other connected-party payments should be supported by written agreements, arm's-length pricing, transfer-pricing records, and applicable Canadian tax filings.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada has no general statutory requirement to surrender export proceeds to a Canadian bank, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no general deadline requiring conversion of foreign-currency receipts. Export proceeds may generally remain in foreign-currency accounts or be converted at the entity's commercial discretion. The partnership should maintain complete invoices, contracts, delivery or performance evidence, customer identity records, receipt reconciliations, and accounting records. Foreign-currency balances and transactions must be recorded under applicable Canadian accounting policies and tax rules. Large cash transactions, suspicious transactions, and certain international electronic funds transfers may trigger FINTRAC reporting by the reporting financial institution; these reporting obligations do not constitute a surrender requirement.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium for payment operations and low-to-medium as a substitute for a Canadian bank account. An offshore electronic-money institution or payment service provider may support foreign-currency collections, virtual accounts, card settlement, and international transfers only within the provider's licensing perimeter and risk policy. It is not automatically a Canadian deposit-taking institution, cannot represent itself as a Canadian bank, and may not provide Canadian-dollar deposit, payment, or money-services functionality without the required Canadian authorization or registration. A non-Canadian money services business serving Canadian persons may have FINTRAC registration and reporting obligations. Customer funds may be safeguarded rather than insured deposits, and account availability can be restricted for Canadian limited partnerships, non-resident partners, advertising-platform flows, high-volume pass-through activity, or third-party settlement. Use a Canadian bank as the primary treasury account and an approved fintech as a documented secondary rail after confirming licensing, safeguarding, settlement, sanctions, chargeback, data, and account-termination terms.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Canadian banks may permit remote onboarding, but no uniform legal right to remote account opening exists. Requirements are bank-specific and depend on the partnership's structure, Canadian nexus, non-resident ownership, expected transaction profile, and risk rating. The bank may require a director, general partner, authorized signatory, beneficial owner, or controlling person to attend a video or in-person interview, provide notarized or certified identification, or visit a branch. An Alberta limited partnership should expect enhanced review where its general partner is foreign, the limited partners are layered entities, the operating team is outside Canada, or receipts and payments are predominantly cross-border. Remote onboarding is more viable when the partnership has a Canadian registered office, a clearly documented general partner, complete corporate and partnership records, Canadian tax identifiers where applicable, transparent ownership, and a credible commercial website and customer contract set.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unclear ownership or control of the limited partnership, including unidentified limited partners, nominee arrangements, layered holding companies, or inability to identify the controlling general partner.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed limited partnership agreement; Alberta registration and certificates; general partner constitutional documents; complete ownership chart to natural persons; beneficial-owner and control-person declarations; certified identity and address evidence; partnership resolutions; authority matrix; and records identifying any person with effective control.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident contribution described only as an investment or capital transfer without a clear legal and commercial purpose.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Capital contribution agreement or partner subscription documentation; limited partnership agreement; source-of-funds evidence; originating bank statements; investor corporate records; audited or management financial statements; tax-residency information; sanctions-screening results; and a written funds-flow memorandum linking the remitter to the partnership.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Programmatic advertising receipts appear to be pass-through funds, involve numerous unrelated advertisers or publishers, or are inconsistent with the stated low-risk business profile.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Platform terms; advertiser and publisher agreements; insertion orders; invoices; payment-flow diagram; reconciliation methodology; fraud and brand-safety controls; customer due-diligence policy; refund and chargeback procedures; sample transaction files; expected monthly volume and jurisdictions; and evidence that the partnership receives only contractual platform revenue or clearly segregated settlement amounts.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-volume international wires, rapid in-and-out movement of funds, payments to unrelated third parties, or transactions involving high-risk jurisdictions.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Rolling cash-flow forecast; approved payment matrix; counterparties and countries register; transaction-purpose descriptions; invoices and contracts; sanctions and adverse-media screening policy; dual-approval procedures; bank reconciliation reports; exception logs; and documented escalation and suspicious-transaction review procedures.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Mismatch between the registered Alberta entity, the actual operating location, tax residence, website, personnel, and customer base.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Registered-office evidence; lease or service-office agreement; operating model memorandum; employee or contractor records; management biographies; website and product documentation; Alberta and federal tax registrations where applicable; customer and vendor lists; and board or partner resolutions approving the Canadian operating model.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Use of foreign payment institutions, virtual accounts, or payment processors without proof of licensing, safeguarding, or contractual authority.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provider licence and registration evidence; service agreement; safeguarding and settlement terms; account ownership confirmation; processor compliance questionnaire; transaction-level reporting; reconciliation controls; data-processing terms; and legal analysis confirming that the arrangement does not constitute unauthorized deposit-taking, money transmission, or securities activity in Canada.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Incomplete tax characterization of partnership distributions, service fees, royalties, interest, or payments to non-resident partners.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Canadian and foreign tax-residency certificates; partner tax forms; partnership tax memorandum; withholding analysis; treaty-benefit documentation; transfer-pricing policy; intercompany agreements; general ledger mapping; and filing calendar for applicable information returns and tax remittances.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Route partner contributions and shareholder or related-party funding through an account held in the legal name of the Alberta limited partnership, using SWIFT or correspondent-bank transfers with the exact legal name, Canadian account details, originating institution, remitter identity, and clear payment narrative such as "limited partnership capital contribution" or "partner loan under agreement dated [date]." Canada generally does not impose standardized foreign-exchange purpose codes for ordinary commercial wires; the bank may nevertheless request an internal purpose classification and supporting documents. Pre-notify the bank for material or unusual receipts. Match each receipt to the executed contribution, subscription, or loan agreement; retain the SWIFT confirmation, remitter bank details, source-of-funds evidence, and ledger posting; and avoid third-party funding unless the relationship and agency basis are documented. Confirm whether the transfer creates Canadian withholding, thin-capitalization, transfer-pricing, foreign-affiliate, partnership allocation, or information-reporting consequences. Do not route capital through personal accounts, undisclosed omnibus wallets, or unrelated collection accounts.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Use SWIFT MT103 or the bank's current ISO 20022 equivalent for identified supplier, publisher, technology, cloud, media, and professional-service payments. Include beneficiary legal name, address, account or IBAN where applicable, BIC or routing information, invoice number, contract reference, and accurate payment purpose. Use commercial letters of credit only where documentary control, supplier-risk mitigation, or trade-finance requirements justify the cost; the issuing bank will require credit approval, facility documentation, compliant shipping or service documents, and sanctions screening. For recurring low-value Canadian payments, use domestic EFT or the bank's approved ACH-equivalent rail; for U.S. payments, use the bank's cross-border ACH or wire service as appropriate. Reconcile settlement files to invoices and approved vendor masters, apply dual authorization, screen beneficiaries and intermediaries, and retain payment evidence. Advertising-platform settlement to publishers should be governed by written terms, verified beneficiary data, tax documentation, fraud controls, and a documented treatment of any funds held or transmitted on behalf of others.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards with a Canadian bank or appropriately authorized dealer, used to hedge forecast or contracted exposures and supported by documented exposure, tenor, notional, counterparty limit, valuation, and settlement controls.

Non-deliverable forwards for currencies or jurisdictions where physical delivery is restricted or impractical, subject to counterparty eligibility, applicable Canadian derivatives rules, reporting, collateral, and close-out documentation.

Cross-currency swaps or currency swaps for identified debt, investment, or recurring operating exposures, subject to ISDA or equivalent documentation, counterparty credit approval, collateral terms, valuation, accounting, and regulatory reporting.

Spot foreign-exchange transactions for ordinary settlement and liquidity management; speculative trading, leveraged products, and instruments lacking a documented underlying exposure should be prohibited under the treasury policy.

Foreign-exchange options or collars may be considered only after confirming the partnership's sophistication, legal capacity, counterparty documentation, accounting treatment, premium funding, suitability, and applicable derivatives regulation.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after each anniversary of the date of registration of the LP declaration
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of CAD $250 per year if filed after the 60-day window; failure to file for two consecutive anniversaries triggers administrative strike-off by the Registrar.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T5013 Partnership Information Return (including T5013 Summary and T5013 slips)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: On or before March 31 of the calendar year immediately following the partnership's taxation year (typically the calendar year)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Penalty under Income Tax Act subsection 162(7) of CAD $25 per day, minimum CAD $100, maximum CAD $2,500; separate penalties per slip under subsection 162(6) up to CAD $25,000 for gross negligence.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Affirmation of Partner Register Accuracy (submitted together with the Annual Return)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Same 60-day anniversary window as the LP Annual Return
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Included in the annual return delinquency regime; false or misleading sworn attestation may expose general partners to liability under the Alberta Partnership Act and criminal sanctions under the Criminal Code.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory audit is imposed solely by Alberta law on a limited partnership; an audit becomes mandatory if the LP is a reporting issuer under securities legislation, if the partnership agreement so requires, if partners holding a majority interest demand an audit, or if the CRA requests audited financial statements under the Income Tax Act.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS as issued by the Accounting Standards Board of Canada, or Canadian Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) for entities that are not publicly accountable.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta's Beneficial Ownership Transparency Act applies to corporations, not limited partnerships. For an Alberta LP, there is no separate annual UBO declaration. However, every transfer of a partnership interest must be recorded in the partnership's register of partners, and the general partner(s) must ensure current beneficial ownership records are maintained at the registered office. CRA may independently require beneficial ownership identification for tax administration purposes.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Transfer of Partnership Interests
Minute Book of Resolutions and Consents

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: LP level: 0% (flow-through); combined federal + Alberta general corporate rate for corporate partners: 23% (federal 15% + Alberta 8%); non-resident partners: 25% Part XIII withholding on treaty-unprotected passive distributions.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No entity-level tax for the Alberta LP; CCPC corporate partners benefit from the small business deduction at a combined 11% (federal 9% + Alberta 2%) on the first C$500,000 of active business income; SR&ED investment tax credits of 15% to 35%; no Alberta capital tax; no statutory tax holiday for AdTech programmatic platforms.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T5013 Summary and T5013 Partnership Information Return; filed electronically by the designated member via CRA NETFILE approved software or CRA My Business Account; corporate partners additionally file the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return via CRA e-file.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (partnership fiscal period capped at 12 months, generally calendar year-end unless grandfathered); separate quarterly GST/HST and payroll remittances apply.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T5013 must be filed within 5 months after the partnership fiscal year-end (e.g., May 31 for a December 31 year-end); T2 return due 6 months after the corporate partner's fiscal year-end; personal partner returns due April 30 (or June 15 for self-employed).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Partnership legal name, CRA business number, agent identifier, fiscal period end, jurisdiction code for Alberta, and mailing address.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Indicate the presence of non-resident partners and list each non-resident's country of residence in the partnership schedule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: All gross advertising exchange and programmatic DSP/SSP revenues, including take rates, media fees, technology service fees, and auction settlement volumes.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report only Canadian-source gross revenue; revenue attributable to a Canadian permanent establishment is taxable in Canada.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Deductible costs: ad servers, data bandwidth, sub-processing fees, platform infrastructure, payroll, rent, marketing, legal, and professional fees.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Expenses must be reasonable and supported by contemporaneous documentation; payments to non-resident affiliates require T106 disclosure and arm's-length pricing.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net partnership income or loss before allocation, computed under Canadian tax rules (ITA 9–37), starting from GAAP net income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-resident partner, the allocable net income, if sourced to a Canadian PE, is subject to Part I tax; passive allocations may attract Part XIII withholding.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Each limited partner's share of income or loss, capital account contributions, allocation percentages, and applicable segregation between active and passive shares.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Provide the non-resident partner's name, taxpayer identification number, and country code; attach Form NR301/NR302 and residence certificates for treaty claims.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Disclosure of aggregate transactions between the partnership and non-resident related parties in the AdTech group, including revenue sharing and technology licenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Complete where aggregate transactions with one non-resident exceed C$1,000,000; maintain transfer pricing documentation for CRA audit.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 4 – GST/HST, Payroll, and Contractor Reporting
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: GST/HST registration and net tax remitted, T4 payroll slips, T5018 contractor statements, and any information returns for payments to agents or sub-publishers.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident LP carrying on business in Canada must register for GST/HST and file under the Simplified or Normal method; Alberta applies 5% GST with no provincial component.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T5013: C$25 per partner per day, minimum C$100, maximum C$2,500; false omission penalty: 50% of unreported amounts under ITA 163(2); corporate T2 late penalty: 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per month up to 12 months; prescribed interest compounded daily on all outstanding amounts.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% under Part XIII for dividends paid by a Canadian corporation; for the Alberta LP, the non-resident partner's Canadian business income share is generally taxed net under Part I where the LP has a Canadian permanent establishment, but passive or guaranteed allocations and distributions that are treaty-unprotected attract Part XIII at 25%, treaty-reduced to 15% (portfolio) or 5% (foreign corporate shareholder holding directly 10% or more of voting rights).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: Before remittance, the non-resident partner must complete CRA Form NR301 (individual) or NR302 (corporate), supply an official Certificate of Residence (e.g., IRS Form 6166 for US partners) to the LP as withholding agent, and recertify annually; the LP must retain the documents, apply the reduced rate on the T5013 summary, remit by the 15th of the month following distribution, and, where over-withheld, the partner claims a refund through a Part I return.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: statutory 25% Part XIII; treaty rates typically 10% for industrial royalties (e.g., Canada–US) and 0% for certain copyright/software royalties under applicable treaties. Interest: arm's-length interest is exempt from domestic withholding under ITA 212(1)(b)(vii); non-arm's-length interest is subject to 25% statutory Part XIII, treaty-reduced to 15% or lower (commonly 0% for certain US arm's-length lenders).

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Form T106 mandatory when aggregate non-arm's-length transactions with a single non-resident exceed C$1,000,000 per taxation year; CRA administrative guidance expects Master File and Local File contemporaneous documentation where Canadian gross revenues exceed C$10,000,000 or the group is in the largest segment; Country-by-Country Report required for multinational groups with consolidated group revenue of at least C$1.25 billion.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not impose Caribbean-style Economic Substance Regulations, but substance is decisive for: (i) LP residence under the central management and control test; (ii) treaty benefits under the Canada–US Limitation on Benefits clause or the MLI Principal Purpose Test; and (iii) GAAR application under ITA 245. The Alberta LP must maintain an active operational presence—local employees, board meetings, contracts, servers, bank accounts, and real commercial risk. A letter-box LP acting as a conduit for non-resident owners will be re-characterized and stripped of treaty relief.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Wilfully omitting programmatic ad revenue, inflating intercompany fees, fabricating T5013 allocations, or shifting profits to non-resident affiliates through sham transactions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Summary conviction: fine of 50% to 200% of tax evaded and imprisonment up to 2 years; indictment: fine of 50% to 200% of tax evaded and imprisonment up to 5 years under ITA 239; civil gross negligence penalty of 50% of unreported tax under ITA 163(2).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: General partners (and directors of a corporate general partner) are jointly and severally liable; directors who knowingly sign or assent to false filings face personal fines, CRA asset seizure, travel bans, and extradition for serious tax offences.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to file Form T106 or maintain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation for cross-border AdTech technology and revenue-sharing transactions priced outside the arm's-length range.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Reassessment under ITA 247 to the arm's-length price; penalty of 10% of the net upward adjustment where the adjustment exceeds the lesser of C$5 million and 10% of gross revenue; interest accrued from the original due date.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Officers and directors may be sued for negligence and misfeasance by co-partners and creditors; knowing participation in mispricing schemes triggers personal liability under the Income Tax Act and possible criminal prosecution.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using a substance-poor Alberta LP solely as a conduit to access treaty benefits and reduce or avoid the 25% Part XIII withholding on programmatic platform profits ultimately owned by non-residents.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: GAAR disallowance under ITA 245, reclassification of distributions as deemed dividends or royalties subject to 25% Part XIII, interest, and penalties; denial of relief under the Limitation on Benefits or Principal Purpose Test; gross negligence penalty of up to 50%.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: General partners and directors may be assessed personally for unremitted withholding under ITA 227.1/227.2; scheme promoters face ITA 163.2 tax-planning penalties up to C$100,000 or 100% of gross fees from the arrangement.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating a clearing or settlement function between advertisers and publishers that constitutes a Money Services Business without FINTRAC registration, or failing to file Suspicious Transaction Reports on programmatic payment flows.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative monetary penalties up to C$1,000,000 for individuals and C$2,000,000 for entities per violation under the PCMLTFA; criminal prosecution and asset forfeiture for money laundering under Criminal Code s.462.31 with imprisonment up to 10 years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors, officers, and general partners with knowledge of unreported suspicious flows face criminal collusion charges, personal disgorgement, and imprisonment; FINTRAC compliance orders may prohibit management roles.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to register and remit 5% GST on taxable B2B programmatic advertising supplies in Alberta, or failing to remit payroll source deductions for Canadian-based staff.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: GST assessment plus 6% annual prescribed interest compounded daily; late remittance penalty of 6% of the amount plus 1% per month; payroll penalties up to 10% of unremitted amounts, increased to 20% for repeated failures.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of a corporate general partner are personally liable for unremitted GST/HST and source deductions under ETA s.323 and ITA s.227.1; CRA may seize personal bank accounts, garnish personal wages, and obtain civil judgments.
